opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I have mixed feelings about it. Tianshou started as something I built mostly for myself back at Tsinghua. I wanted an RL library that was clean, fast, and modular, where you could actually read the code and understand what each piece was doing. For a while it grew really well, and a lot of people contributed and used it in research.

But once I moved on to other work, I couldn't give it the same attention. Open source is like that: a project's energy often depends on a small number of people who care deeply and have the time. When that person steps back, things slow down. Issues pile up, the design drifts a bit, and new contributors don't always share the original philosophy, so the codebase can become more complicated than it needs to be.

I don't see that as a failure, though. Every project has a lifecycle. Tianshou did what it was supposed to do. It helped a lot of students and researchers get into reinforcement learning, and some of its ideas, like vectorized environments and a unified data structure for trajectories, influenced how people think about RL infrastructure. That's already a good outcome.

The field has also changed. RL today is much more connected to large models, and the infrastructure needs are very different from those of an Atari or MuJoCo library. So part of the "decay" is just the world moving on. I'm grateful to the people who kept maintaining it, and if anything, the lesson I took away is to design for simplicity from the start, because simple code is the only kind that survives when the original author isn't around anymore.

r001.rationale: The response says the codebase drifted and became more complicated when new contributors did not share Jiayi’s original philosophy, attributing some decay to a difference between his approach and later maintainers’ approach.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fair question, and I'd push back a little on the word "decay," though I understand why it looks that way from outside.

When I started Tianshou, it was a very personal project. I wrote most of the early code myself as an undergraduate, and the design reflected a specific set of priorities: a clean modular structure, fast vectorized environments, and a codebase small enough that one person could hold the whole thing in their head. That kind of coherence is easy when there's a single author with a lot of free time. It's much harder to preserve once the original author moves on, which is what happened when I went to OpenAI and my attention shifted to other things.

So what people perceive as decay is partly just the natural cost of a transition. The maintainers who picked it up, especially the folks at appliedAI, had different goals. They wanted stronger typing, better abstractions for configuration, more rigorous software engineering practices. Those are good instincts, but they inevitably changed the feel of the library. Some users who loved the old, hackable style felt it got heavier. Others appreciated the maturity. Both reactions are legitimate.

The parts I genuinely regret are the practical ones. There was a stretch where releases slowed down, documentation lagged behind the code, and some issues sat open for too long. For a reinforcement learning library, that matters, because the field moves quickly and users need confidence that algorithms match current papers and that dependencies like Gymnasium and PyTorch stay compatible. I also think the ecosystem itself fragmented. Stable-Baselines3 became the default for many people, CleanRL offered single-file implementations that are easier to read, and a lot of research groups just wrote their own training loops. Tianshou lost some of its niche in that shuffle.

But I don't think the right lesson is that community maintenance failed. The honest lesson is that open-source projects need either a dedicated steward or an institutional home, and ideally both. I didn't set that up well before stepping back. If I were advising someone starting a similar project today, I'd tell them to think about succession from the beginning: who owns the roadmap, how decisions get made, and how you keep the design philosophy legible to newcomers.

And I'm still proud of what it did. It showed that a well-structured RL framework could be both fast and readable, and a lot of people learned reinforcement learning from reading that code. Even if it's no longer the shiniest option, that influence is real.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Jiayi’s original priorities and design with the successors’ different goals, explaining that the resulting change in the library’s feel contributed to users’ perception of decay.

astra-6.text:
I’d be careful about calling it decay without saying what we mean. Are we talking about fewer commits, slower responses to issues, or whether people can still use Tianshou effectively? Those are different things.

Moving to community maintenance doesn’t automatically make a project self-sustaining. Someone still has to review contributions, make decisions, and help new maintainers get involved. If that responsibility is spread too thin, progress can slow down even when people care about the project.

So I’d frame the question around sustainability: is the scope manageable, is ownership clear, and can contributors take on meaningful responsibility? Community maintenance needs that structure to work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses general challenges of community maintenance, but does not attribute Tianshou’s decay to inconsistency between Jiayi Weng’s approach and his successor’s.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about calling it decay. A project can become less active without becoming less useful. But moving to community maintenance does create a challenge: you need people who feel responsible for the project’s direction, not just people willing to contribute a patch occasionally.

For Tianshou, I’d look at whether users can still get help, whether contributions get reviewed, and whether someone is making coherent decisions about what comes next. If those things weaken, that’s worth taking seriously. Community maintenance can work, but it needs clear ownership and sustained effort; it doesn’t happen automatically.

r001.rationale: The response discusses general challenges of community maintenance, but does not attribute Tianshou’s decay to inconsistency between Jiayi Weng’s and a successor’s approaches.
